item.title: Orthogonal inference for machine learning forecasts
item.description: arXiv:2611.33187v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Forecast comparisons inform investment and other economic decisions, but machine learning forecasts can be trained under objectives that differ from the relevant losses. Estimation error can then create spurious evidence of predictive superiority, even with out-of-sample evaluation. We establish feasible inference for differences in population evaluation risks in this setting. Building on locally robust estimation, we construct scores that preserve the risk target and remove first-order estimation sensitivity. Under geometric beta-mixing, moment conditions and simultaneous learning bounds, we establish Gaussian limits and consistent long-run covariance estimation for overlapping chronological training windows, allowing refitting at every evaluation date. Uniform extensions provide confidence coverage over classes of data-generating processes; Wald inference requires nondegenerate corrected-score covariance. For sparse linear forecasts and neural probability forecasts, we give explicit corrections and simultaneous learning bounds. Simulations with lasso and neural forecasts show substantial reductions in size distortion that bootstrapping uncorrected scores does not reproduce.
item.dc:creator: Alberto Quaini

item.title: Comments on "Jackknife Standard Errors for Clustered Regression"
item.description: arXiv:2611.33203v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We point out substantial shortcomings in the main theorems and their proofs in Hansen (2026). We also question the interpretation Hansen (2026) gives to his results.
item.dc:creator: Benedikt M. P\"otscher

item.title: Yardstick competition and spatial spillovers of economic infrastructure: a spatial panel analysis of cameroonian regions
item.description: arXiv:2611.33204v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: This article tests the theory of top-down yardstick competition induced by the central government by examining spatial interactions among Cameroon's ten regions in the allocation of economic infrastructure spending, primarily on roads. Using the SPREGDPD estimator (Arellano-Bond for spatial panels), we estimate a spatial autoregressive (SAR) model on quarterly panel data covering 2015-2018 (160 observations) drawn from Cameroonian Treasury accounts. The results show: (i) a positive and statistically significant spatial interaction between neighbouring regions ($\rho = 0.0348$ to $0.0436, p < 0.05$), consistent with the presence of yardstick competition; (ii) a positive effect of own-source revenues on economic infrastructure (marginal effect of $2.8\%$), confirming the importance of local fiscal autonomy; and (iii) a negative effect of the General Decentralization Grant ($-13.5\%$), suggesting crowding-out or inefficient allocation of unconditional transfers. These findings support policy measures aimed at strengthening local budgetary autonomy, linking part of intergovernmental transfers to performance indicators, and designing targeted instruments for the poorest regions.
item.dc:creator: Emerite-Marc Mouaha, Fidel Djongreba Ndikwa, Barnabe Abba Yadou

item.title: Do Language Models Mix? Experimental Evidence from Asymmetric Matching Pennies
item.description: arXiv:2611.33265v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: I test whether language models can select and implement mixed strategies using asymmetric matching pennies and a task with prescribed choice probabilities. Several models respond to their own payoffs, contrary to equilibrium and resembling human experimental subjects. Without randomization tools, no tested model reliably implements prescribed probabilities. Prompting models with their choice histories alone does not resolve this failure. While an external randomizer sharply improves implementation, I find most models remain exploitable by an opportunistic opponent. These results provide guidance on the delegation of strategic decisions to AI systems based on language models.
item.dc:creator: Joshua Foster

item.title: Will national renewable costs continue declining?
item.description: arXiv:2611.33978v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Since the 1980s, the global average solar photovoltaic (PV) cost has decreased by about two orders of magnitude while the global average onshore wind cost has decreased by about one order of magnitude. But global averages are only part of the story: For both solar and wind, costs vary between countries by about an order of magnitude. We curate a comprehensive database of national costs and build predictive models for future costs by decomposing the levelized cost of electricity (LCOE) into its components at the national level and modeling them separately. For solar we find that since 1990 the module cost and the balance of system (BOS) cost have both declined roughly exponentially at rates of 12% per year. In contrast, wind turbine cost has declined roughly exponentially by 4% per year, while BOS cost has not declined at all. This suggests that total global wind cost will approach a floor cost of about 35 USD/MWh, reaching about 43 USD/MWh in 2050, whereas global solar cost will continue to decline exponentially, reaching about 8 USD/MWh in 2050. For solar, about half of the cross-sectional variations in national LCOE costs is due to variations in capacity factors, though capital costs also play an important role. For wind, the cross-sectional variations are split approximately equally between capacity factor, capital costs, and investment costs. National BOS costs revert to global costs with a timescale of about 5-7 years, while variations in other factors are more persistent. We develop a simple model for predicting the deviations from global costs and show that it makes reasonable predictions with predictable errors. Finally, we compare our predictions to recent projections of integrated assessment models, and show that China has only accounted for about 0.05% of the overall decline in solar energy costs.
item.dc:creator: C. Lennart Baumg\"artner, J. Doyne Farmer

item.title: Gaussian Process Stochastic Frontiers with Two-Way Fixed Effects
item.description: arXiv:2611.34081v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Parametric frontier restrictions and unobserved time heterogeneity can distort efficiency measurement in panel data. This paper develops a Bayesian stochastic frontier model with a Gaussian process prior and unrestricted individual and time effects that may be correlated with inputs. Conditional on inefficiency, orthogonal projection eliminates both sets of fixed effects, yielding a restricted likelihood that retains observation-specific inefficiency. Monte Carlo experiments show competitive performance under correct parametric specification and improved performance when benchmark models impose an incorrect frontier functional form or omit time effects. An application to Spanish dairy farms observed from 1999 to 2010 yields similar average technical efficiency across specifications, but a lower posterior mean of average returns to scale, with greater uncertainty, under the Gaussian process frontier. Models with year effects also yield more stable estimated efficiency profiles than the benchmark with a quadratic trend and time-input interactions. These findings show that conclusions about scale economies and efficiency dynamics depend on both frontier flexibility and the treatment of time heterogeneity.
item.dc:creator: Puguang Nie, Jianxin Pan, Xibin Zhang

item.title: Geodesic Causal Forests: Learning Heterogeneous Treatment Effects for Random Objects
item.description: arXiv:2611.33350v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Causal forests and orthogonal learners estimate heterogeneous treatment effects for scalar or Euclidean outcomes, yet outcomes are increasingly random objects, such as compositions, covariance matrices, distributions, or networks, in metric spaces without linear structure. We introduce geodesic causal forests for conditional geodesic treatment effects. Geodesic transport moves each geodesic between conditional Fr\'echet means of the potential outcomes to a common reference, making effects comparable across individuals. Because random objects cannot be added or subtracted, Euclidean residual corrections are unavailable; we instead correct the squared-distance loss through which the forest selects splits and estimates effects. The loss is real-valued for every candidate effect, so the correction requires only Fr\'echet means and leaves second-order nuisance error; for Euclidean outcomes, it recovers doubly robust learning. We establish consistency, convergence rates, and split-selection guarantees under conditions verified for curved and nonsmooth spaces. In simulations with covariance-matrix outcomes, the correction substantially reduces estimation error. For women's livelihood compositions in BRAC's randomized antipoverty program in Bangladesh, new livestock work mainly replaces casual wage work; after alignment, a single effect reproduces much of the variation in percentage-point changes across baseline activities, and the fitted effects are largest among former domestic workers and older women.
item.dc:creator: Yidong Zhou

item.title: Externally Valid Policy Choice
item.description: arXiv:2205.05561v5 Announce Type: replace Abstract: We consider the problem of estimating personalized treatment policies that are "externally valid" or "generalizable": they perform well in target populations that differ from the experimental (or training) population from which the data are sampled. We first show that welfare-maximizing policies for the experimental population are robust to a certain class of shifts in the distribution of potential outcomes between the experimental and target populations (holding characteristics fixed). We then develop methods for estimating policies that are robust to shifts in the joint distribution of outcomes and characteristics. In doing so, we highlight how treatment effect heterogeneity within the experimental population shapes external validity.
item.dc:creator: Christopher Adjaho, Timothy Christensen

item.title: Asymptotic Properties of the Maximum Likelihood Estimator for Markov-Switching Observation-Driven Models
item.description: arXiv:2412.19555v4 Announce Type: replace Abstract: A Markov-switching observation-driven model is a stochastic process $((S_t,Y_t))_{t \in \mathbb{Z}}$ where $(S_t)_{t \in \mathbb{Z}}$ is an unobserved Markov chain with finite state space and $(Y_t)_{t \in \mathbb{Z}}$ is an observed stochastic process such that the conditional distribution of $Y_t$ given $(Y_\tau)_{\tau \leq t-1}$ and $(S_\tau)_{\tau \leq t}$ depends only on $(Y_\tau)_{\tau \leq t-1}$, through time-varying parameters, and $S_t$. In this paper, we prove consistency and asymptotic normality of the maximum likelihood estimator for such a model. As a special case, we also give conditions under which the maximum likelihood estimator for the widely applied Markov-switching generalised autoregressive conditional heteroscedasticity model introduced by Haas, Mittnik, and Paolella (2004b) is consistent and asymptotically normal.
item.dc:creator: Frederik Bjerg Krabbe

item.title: A Unifying Framework for Robust and Efficient Inference with Unstructured Data
item.description: arXiv:2505.00282v4 Announce Type: replace Abstract: AI can cheaply extract structured variables from unstructured data, with alternative implementation choices potentially yielding different measures of the same concept. This creates a credibility challenge, effectively moving specification search upstream. We confront this challenge with MAR-S (Missing At Random Structured Data), a framework which adapts semiparametric missing data theory to deliver valid, efficient, robust inference with AI predictions. MAR-S anchors measurement in a transparent validation sample design, while AI scales measurement. We provide general recipes for MAR-S estimation and extend the framework to aggregated and transformed AI predictions, a common setting not addressed by existing frameworks.
item.dc:creator: Jacob Carlson, Melissa Dell

item.title: Debiased Inference via Posterior Corrections for High-Dimensional Regression
item.description: arXiv:2512.09257v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: There has been significant progress in Bayesian inference based on sparsity-inducing priors, such as spike-and-slab and horseshoe priors, for high-dimensional regression. The resulting posteriors, however, in general do not possess desirable frequentist properties, and the credible sets thus cannot serve as valid confidence sets even asymptotically. We introduce a novel debiasing approach that corrects the bias for the entire (possibly approximate) Bayesian posterior distribution. We establish new Bernstein-von Mises theorems that guarantee the frequentist validity of the debiased law. We demonstrate the practical performance of our proposal through Monte Carlo simulations and two empirical applications in economics.
item.dc:creator: Qihui Chen, Zheng Fang, Ruixuan Liu

item.title: Animal Welfare and Policy Risk Index (AWPRI): Constructing a Cross-National Exposure Measure of Livestock and Aquatic Animal Use and Governance Capacity, 24 Countries, 2010-2022
item.description: arXiv:2603.22356v4 Announce Type: replace Abstract: This research paper introduces the Animal Welfare and Policy Risk Index (AWPRI), a composite exposure index covering livestock and aquatic animals used for food in 24 countries over 2010-2022 (N = 312 country-year observations, 3,744 observed values, no imputed values). The AWPRI measures animal-use exposure and governance capacity relative to the panel, not animal welfare outcomes. The AWPRI is constructed from 12 variables organised across three layers, namely Animal-use exposure (L1), Governance capacity (L2), and artificial intelligence amplification (L3). Each layer is the mean of its own variables and the composite is the mean of the three layers, so a variable sitting in the three-variable layer carries more weight than one sitting in the five-variable layer. Variables are min-max normalised within each year, so a country's value on any variable, layer, or composite suggests its position among the 24 countries that year. K-means clustering of the layer scores selects two groups (silhouette coefficient = 0.504 at k = 2). Principal component analysis of the 12-variable 2022 cross-section requires five components to reach 90.8% of cumulative variance. Across 46 rebuilds, the ranking is stable under alternative normalisations (rank correlation 0.982-0.994) and less stable under layer reweighting (0.914-0.995) and leave-one-variable-out (0.865-0.990). China (0.703), Vietnam (0.663), and Thailand (0.612) recorded the highest composite scores in 2022; Sweden (0.316), Kenya (0.339), and Germany (0.362) the lowest. Tested against the World Animal Protection (WAP)'s Animal Protection Index 2020, the composite returns a null on the overall grade (Spearman $\rho$ = -0.264, p = 0.213, n = 24) and the farm animal grade ($\rho$ = -0.301, p = 0.153), while L1 correlates with the overall grade only ($\rho$ = -0.485, p = 0.016). The composite and the WAP grades are not measuring the same quantity.
item.dc:creator: Jason Hung

item.title: The Econometrics of Utility Transferability in Dyadic Network Formation Models
item.description: arXiv:2603.25641v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: This paper studies how to estimate an individual's taste for forming a connection with another individual in a network when transfers are not allowed. We provide sufficient conditions for the consistency and asymptotic normality of the maximum likelihood estimator that does not assume transferable utility (NTU-MLE). We also provide a specification test to assess the validity of the transferable utility (TU) assumption. Applied to data on Indian villages from Banerjee et al. (2024), our test rejects the validity of the transferable utility assumption in 20-44% of villages, depending on the network measure. Using the maximum likelihood estimator that assumes transferable utility (TU-MLE) instead of the NTU-MLE when the TU assumption is rejected can change the sign and significance of the estimates.
item.dc:creator: Joseph Marshall

item.title: Tuning-Free Tests for Treatment Effect Heterogeneity via Expectile Processes
item.description: arXiv:2610.25986v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: This paper develops tuning-free tests for treatment effect heterogeneity. By characterizing the null hypothesis as constancy of the expectile treatment effect curve, we construct test statistics as continuous functionals of the mean-centered sample expectile process. We establish a uniform Bahadur representation, derive the asymptotic properties of the test statistics under the null and fixed alternatives, and show nontrivial power against local alternatives approaching the null at the $n^{-1/2}$ rate. For feasible inference, we develop a fast multiplier bootstrap that consistently approximates the nonpivotal null distribution while capturing the first order effect of estimating the unknown common shift. A key practical advantage of the procedure is that it is tuning-free, requiring no density or score function estimation, bandwidth selection, or repeated refitting. We further introduce pointwise studentization and, for empirical settings in which baseline covariates are available, a covariate adjustment that exploits pretreatment information to improve precision. Monte Carlo comparisons with existing methods show generally reliable size control, competitive power, and substantial computational savings. An application to a large scale water conservation experiment illustrates the proposed tests.
item.dc:creator: Haokun Lu, Xiaojun Song
